title: Linear Models
description: The foundational algorithms: predicting numbers with linear regression, predicting categories with logistic regression, keeping both honest with regularization and basic metrics.

lessons.title: Linear Regression
lessons.description: Learn the simplest, most foundational algorithm for predicting a number.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain how linear regression works and train a simple model with scikit-learn.

sections.title: 📈 The core idea
sections.content:
**Linear regression** predicts a numeric value as a weighted sum of the input features, plus a constant — fitting the best straight line (or flat plane, in higher dimensions) through the data.

```
price = w1 * square_feet + w2 * bedrooms + b
```

Training means finding the weights (`w1`, `w2`, ...) and bias (`b`) that make the line's predictions as close as possible to the actual training values.

sections.title: 📏 How "best fit" is measured
sections.content:
Linear regression typically minimizes the **mean squared error** — the average of the squared differences between predicted and actual values. Squaring the errors punishes big misses more than small ones, and keeps errors from cancelling each other out.

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

predictions = model.predict(X_test)
print(model.coef_)        # the learned weights
print(model.intercept_)   # the learned bias term
```

sections.title: ✅ When linear regression works well
sections.content:
Linear regression is simple, fast, and easy to interpret (each weight tells you roughly how much that feature matters). It works best when the true relationship between features and the target is genuinely close to linear.

• Great baseline — always worth trying before something more complex
• Coefficients are directly interpretable: "each extra bedroom adds about $15,000"
• Struggles when the real relationship is strongly non-linear or has complex interactions between features

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Using linear regression on clearly non-linear relationships without adjustment.** A straight line can't capture a curved relationship — features may need transforming, or a different model may be needed.

**Ignoring feature scale.** Features on very different scales can make the learned coefficients harder to interpret directly (though the predictions themselves are unaffected for plain linear regression).

**Not checking residuals.** Plotting the errors (predicted minus actual) can reveal patterns the model is systematically missing.

questions.question: What does linear regression predict?
options: A category label
A numeric value, as a weighted sum of the input features
A cluster assignment
A probability distribution over classes
questions.explanation: Linear regression outputs a continuous number — it fits a linear combination of the input features (weights times features, plus a bias) to predict that number.

questions.question: Why does linear regression typically minimize squared error rather than raw error?
options: Squaring makes the math impossible to solve
Squaring punishes larger errors more heavily and prevents positive and negative errors from cancelling out
Squared error is always smaller than raw error
There's no real reason — either works identically
questions.explanation: Using squared error means big mistakes are penalized disproportionately more than small ones, and since every squared error is non-negative, errors can't cancel each other out when averaged.

questions.question: What's a key advantage of linear regression over more complex models?
options: It always achieves the highest possible accuracy
Its learned coefficients are directly interpretable, showing roughly how much each feature matters
It requires no training data at all
It works well on any type of relationship, linear or not
questions.explanation: Because linear regression is just a weighted sum, each coefficient has a clear, interpretable meaning — a major advantage in situations where understanding *why* matters, not just the prediction itself.

questions.question: What key assumption does basic linear regression make about the relationship between features and the target?
options: That the relationship is exponential
That the relationship is approximately linear — a straight-line combination of the features
That there's no relationship at all
That the target must be categorical
questions.explanation: Linear regression assumes the target can be reasonably approximated as a weighted linear combination of the input features.

questions.question: What does 'multiple linear regression' refer to?
options: Running linear regression multiple times on the same single feature
Linear regression using more than one input feature to predict the target
A technique unrelated to standard linear regression
Predicting multiple different targets from one feature
questions.explanation: Multiple linear regression simply extends the same idea to more than one predictor variable, combining several features into the prediction.

questions.question: What does the intercept term in a linear regression model represent?
options: The slope of the line
The predicted value when all input features are zero
The model's overall accuracy
The number of features used
questions.explanation: The intercept is the baseline prediction the model makes when every feature's value is zero, before any feature contributions are added.

questions.question: When does plain linear regression tend to underperform?
options: When the true relationship between features and target is strongly non-linear
When the target variable is numeric
When there is exactly one feature
Linear regression always performs equally well regardless of the data
questions.explanation: Because linear regression only captures straight-line relationships, it struggles when the real pattern in the data is curved or otherwise non-linear.

questions.question: How is linear regression's coefficients typically found?
options: Only through trial and error with no formula
Either via a closed-form mathematical solution or iteratively through gradient descent, both minimizing the squared error
By randomly guessing until the loss looks acceptable
Coefficients are always fixed and never learned from data
questions.explanation: Linear regression can be solved directly with a closed-form formula for smaller problems, or iteratively via gradient descent for larger ones — both aim to minimize squared error.

lessons.title: Logistic Regression
lessons.description: Learn how a close cousin of linear regression handles classification instead of predicting a raw number.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain how logistic regression turns a linear combination of features into a class probability.

sections.title: ❓ Why not just use linear regression for classification?
sections.content: For a yes/no prediction (like "will this customer churn?"), you need an output between 0 and 1 that behaves like a probability. Plain linear regression can output any number — including negative values or numbers above 1 — which doesn't make sense as a probability.

sections.title: 📉 The sigmoid function
sections.content:
**Logistic regression** solves this by taking the same weighted sum as linear regression, then squashing it through the **sigmoid function**, which maps any number into the range (0, 1).

```python
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

print(sigmoid(0))     # 0.5   — right at the decision boundary
print(sigmoid(5))     # ~0.99 — very confident "yes"
print(sigmoid(-5))    # ~0.01 — very confident "no"
```

A prediction above 0.5 (by default) is classified as the positive class; below 0.5, the negative class.

sections.title: 🎯 Training and using logistic regression
sections.content:
```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

model = LogisticRegression()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

probabilities = model.predict_proba(X_test)  # probability of each class
predictions = model.predict(X_test)          # the final 0/1 class
```

• Despite the name, logistic regression is a **classification** algorithm, not a regression one
• Like linear regression, it's a strong, fast, interpretable baseline for classification tasks

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Being confused by the name.** "Logistic regression" sounds like regression, but it's used for classification — the name refers to the math (the logistic/sigmoid function), not the task.

**Always using the default 0.5 threshold.** For imbalanced problems (like rare fraud detection), a different threshold often works better — this is a tunable choice, not a fixed rule.

**Treating the output probability as perfectly calibrated.** It's a useful confidence signal, but "70% probability" doesn't always mean exactly 70% of such cases are truly positive without additional calibration.

questions.question: Why can't plain linear regression be used directly for a yes/no classification problem?
options: Linear regression can't be trained on binary data at all
Its output isn't bounded between 0 and 1, so it doesn't behave like a valid probability
Linear regression is too slow for classification
There's no actual issue — it works identically
questions.explanation: Linear regression can output any real number, including values below 0 or above 1 — which don't make sense as probabilities, so a squashing function is needed.

questions.question: What does the sigmoid function do in logistic regression?
options: It removes outliers from the training data
It maps the linear combination of features into a value between 0 and 1, interpretable as a probability
It computes the mean squared error
It selects which features to use
questions.explanation: The sigmoid function takes any real-valued input (the weighted sum of features) and squashes it into the range (0, 1), producing something that behaves like a probability.

questions.question: Despite its name, what type of task is logistic regression used for?
options: Predicting a continuous numeric value
Classification — predicting a category or class
Clustering unlabeled data
Reinforcement learning
questions.explanation: Logistic regression is a classification algorithm — the "regression" in the name refers to fitting a linear combination of features, not to predicting a continuous number.

questions.question: What decision threshold is commonly used to convert a logistic regression's probability output into a class prediction?
options: Always exactly the average of the training labels
0.5 by default — probabilities above it predict one class, below predict the other
Whatever value makes accuracy exactly 100%
There's no threshold; probabilities are the final output
questions.explanation: A common default is to predict the positive class if the estimated probability is above 0.5, though this threshold can be adjusted for specific needs.

questions.question: What loss function is commonly used to train logistic regression?
options: Mean squared error, exactly like linear regression
Log loss (cross-entropy loss), which penalizes confident wrong predictions especially heavily
There is no loss function used in logistic regression
Accuracy is used directly as the loss function
questions.explanation: Logistic regression is typically trained using log loss, which strongly penalizes predictions that are both confident and wrong.

questions.question: Can logistic regression be extended beyond binary (two-class) classification?
options: No, it can only ever handle exactly two classes
Yes, through extensions like multinomial (softmax) logistic regression for multiple classes
Only by converting it into a decision tree
Multiclass problems require an entirely unrelated algorithm
questions.explanation: Logistic regression generalizes to multiple classes through approaches like multinomial logistic regression, which extends the same underlying idea.

questions.question: How can a logistic regression coefficient be interpreted in terms of odds?
options: Coefficients have no interpretable meaning at all
A coefficient reflects how the log-odds of the positive class change with a one-unit increase in that feature
Coefficients only indicate the number of training examples
They represent the exact predicted probability directly
questions.explanation: Because logistic regression models the log-odds as a linear function of the features, each coefficient shows how a feature shifts those log-odds.

questions.question: What kind of output does logistic regression naturally produce, before any thresholding?
options: A single hard class label only
A continuous probability estimate between 0 and 1
A cluster assignment
A ranking of all possible classes with no numeric value
questions.explanation: Logistic regression's raw output is a probability score, which is then optionally converted into a hard class label using a threshold.

lessons.title: Regularization: Keeping Models from Overfitting
lessons.description: Learn how a simple penalty term helps linear models resist memorizing noise.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what regularization does and describe the difference between L1 and L2 regularization.

sections.title: 🎛️ Why penalize large weights?
sections.content: A model with very large weights tends to be extremely sensitive to small changes in its inputs — a hallmark of overfitting. **Regularization** adds a penalty to the training process that discourages weights from growing too large, nudging the model toward simpler, more generalizable solutions.

sections.title: 📏 L2 regularization (Ridge)
sections.content:
**L2 regularization** (used in **Ridge regression**) adds a penalty proportional to the *squared* size of the weights. This shrinks all weights smoothly toward zero, without necessarily making any of them exactly zero.

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

model = Ridge(alpha=1.0)  # alpha controls how strong the penalty is
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
```

sections.title: 📐 L1 regularization (Lasso)
sections.content:
**L1 regularization** (used in **Lasso regression**) adds a penalty proportional to the *absolute* size of the weights. A useful side effect: it can push some weights all the way to exactly zero — effectively performing automatic feature selection.

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso

model = Lasso(alpha=1.0)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(model.coef_)  # some coefficients may be exactly 0.0
```

• Use **L2 (Ridge)** when you believe most features matter somewhat
• Use **L1 (Lasso)** when you suspect many features are irrelevant and want automatic feature selection

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Setting the regularization strength (`alpha`) without tuning it.** Too little regularization doesn't help with overfitting; too much causes underfitting — this is typically tuned using the validation set.

**Forgetting to scale features before regularization.** Since the penalty is based on the size of the weights, unscaled features (one ranging 0-1, another 0-100000) get penalized unevenly.

**Assuming regularization always improves performance.** It helps specifically when overfitting is the problem — on a model that's already underfitting, it can make things worse.

questions.question: What problem does regularization primarily help address?
options: Slow training speed
Overfitting — by discouraging overly large weights that make a model too sensitive to training data
Missing values in the dataset
Choosing which algorithm to use
questions.explanation: Regularization adds a penalty for large weights during training, nudging the model toward simpler solutions that are less likely to overfit the training data's noise.

questions.question: What's a distinctive practical effect of L1 (Lasso) regularization?
options: It can push some feature weights to exactly zero, effectively performing feature selection
It always produces a worse fit than no regularization
It only works on classification problems
It requires no tuning parameter at all
questions.explanation: Unlike L2, which shrinks weights smoothly toward zero, L1 regularization can zero out some weights entirely — a useful side effect that automatically drops less useful features.

questions.question: Why does the regularization strength (`alpha`) typically need to be tuned rather than set once and forgotten?
options: alpha has no real effect on the model
Too little regularization doesn't address overfitting, while too much causes underfitting — the right value depends on the specific dataset
alpha only affects training speed
It's automatically set correctly by scikit-learn every time
questions.explanation: There's a sweet spot: not enough regularization leaves overfitting unaddressed, while too much regularization oversimplifies the model and causes underfitting — tuning against a validation set finds the right balance.

questions.question: How does L2 (Ridge) regularization typically affect model weights, compared to L1?
options: It pushes weights to exactly zero, just like L1
It shrinks weights toward zero smoothly without usually setting them to exactly zero
It has no effect on weights at all
It only affects the intercept term
questions.explanation: L2 regularization tends to shrink all weights somewhat but rarely forces any of them to become exactly zero, unlike L1.

questions.question: What's the key mathematical difference between the L1 and L2 penalty terms?
options: They are identical formulas with different names
L1 penalizes the sum of absolute weight values; L2 penalizes the sum of squared weight values
L1 only applies to classification, L2 only to regression
Neither penalty involves the model's weights at all
questions.explanation: L1 regularization adds a penalty proportional to the sum of absolute values of the weights, while L2 adds a penalty proportional to the sum of their squares.

questions.question: What does Elastic Net regularization do?
options: It removes all regularization from the model
It combines both L1 and L2 penalties, blending feature selection with smooth weight shrinkage
It only works for unsupervised learning problems
It's a completely unrelated technique to L1 and L2
questions.explanation: Elastic Net mixes L1 and L2 penalties together, aiming to get the feature-selecting benefit of L1 along with the stability of L2.

questions.question: Where does the regularization penalty get added when training a model?
options: It's applied only after training is fully complete
It's added directly to the loss function being minimized during training, discouraging large weights alongside fitting the data
It replaces the loss function entirely
It's applied only to the test set evaluation
questions.explanation: Regularization works by adding an extra penalty term to the loss function itself, so the optimizer balances fitting the data against keeping weights small.

questions.question: When might regularization be unnecessary for a model?
options: It's always necessary for every model, with no exceptions
When the model is simple relative to the amount of training data and isn't showing signs of overfitting
Regularization is only relevant for unsupervised learning
When the dataset has fewer than 2 features
questions.explanation: If a model already generalizes well and shows no overfitting symptoms — especially with a simple model and plenty of data — heavy regularization may add little benefit.

lessons.title: Evaluating Regression and Classification Models
lessons.description: Learn the essential first metrics for checking whether a model's predictions are actually good.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can compute and interpret basic evaluation metrics for both regression and classification models.

sections.title: 📏 Regression metrics
sections.content:
For predicting numbers, common metrics compare predictions to actual values:

```python
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, r2_score

mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, predictions)
mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, predictions)
r2 = r2_score(y_test, predictions)
```

• **MAE (Mean Absolute Error)** — average absolute difference; easy to interpret in the original units
• **MSE (Mean Squared Error)** — average squared difference; penalizes large errors more heavily
• **R²** — the fraction of variance in the target explained by the model (1.0 = perfect, 0.0 = no better than always predicting the average)

sections.title: ✅ Classification metrics: accuracy
sections.content:
For predicting categories, the simplest metric is **accuracy** — the fraction of predictions that were correct.

```python
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, predictions)
```

Accuracy is intuitive, but it can be seriously misleading on **imbalanced** data — if 95% of transactions are legitimate, a model that always predicts "legitimate" gets 95% accuracy while catching zero fraud.

sections.title: 🎯 Why one metric usually isn't the whole story
sections.content: Different metrics highlight different kinds of mistakes. MAE and MSE disagree on how much to punish large errors; accuracy alone hides *what kind* of mistakes a classifier makes. Picking the right metric (or a small set of complementary ones) for the actual business problem matters more than optimizing a single default number — this gets a full deep dive in a later module.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Relying on accuracy alone for an imbalanced classification problem.** A high accuracy score can hide a model that's completely failing at the thing you actually care about.

**Comparing MSE across datasets with very different target scales.** A "good" MSE for predicting house prices in dollars looks huge compared to one for predicting a 0-1 probability — MSE isn't directly comparable across different problems.

**Reporting only one metric without context.** A single number rarely tells the full story — pairing metrics (like MAE alongside R²) usually paints a clearer picture.

questions.question: Why can accuracy be a misleading metric for an imbalanced classification problem?
options: Accuracy can't be computed for imbalanced data
A model that always predicts the majority class can score high accuracy while being useless for the minority class you actually care about
Accuracy only works for regression problems
Imbalanced data always breaks the accuracy calculation
questions.explanation: On heavily imbalanced data, always predicting the common class yields high accuracy without the model doing anything useful for detecting the rare, often more important, class.

questions.question: What does an R² score of 0.0 indicate about a regression model?
options: The model makes perfect predictions
The model performs no better than simply always predicting the average of the target
The model has a bug and can't be evaluated
The model has zero training data
questions.explanation: R² measures how much of the target's variance the model explains beyond just guessing the average every time — a score of 0.0 means it offers no improvement over that naive baseline.

questions.question: Why do MSE and MAE sometimes give different impressions of a model's error?
options: They are actually identical calculations
MSE squares the errors, so it penalizes large mistakes much more heavily than MAE does
MAE can only be used for classification
MSE ignores small errors entirely
questions.explanation: Because MSE squares each error before averaging, a few large errors have an outsized effect on MSE compared to MAE, which treats all error sizes proportionally — so a model with a few big misses can look worse under MSE than under MAE.

questions.question: What does an R² score of 1.0 indicate about a regression model?
options: The model performs no better than predicting the average
The model perfectly explains all the variance in the target variable on the evaluated data
The model has failed to train
R² of 1.0 is mathematically impossible
questions.explanation: An R² of 1.0 means the model's predictions perfectly match the actual values, explaining all the variability in the target for that data.

questions.question: How is Mean Absolute Error (MAE) calculated?
options: The sum of squared differences between predictions and actual values
The average of the absolute differences between predictions and actual values
The percentage of exactly correct predictions
The largest single error observed
questions.explanation: MAE averages the absolute value of each prediction's error, giving equal weight to every mistake regardless of direction.

questions.question: What does 'accuracy' measure for a classification model?
options: The average distance between predicted and actual numeric values
The fraction of all predictions that exactly matched the true label
The model's training speed
The number of features used
questions.explanation: Accuracy is simply the proportion of predictions that were correct out of all predictions made.

questions.question: Why do regression and classification problems generally require different evaluation metrics?
options: They don't — the same metrics always apply to both
Regression predicts continuous numbers (needing metrics like MSE or R²), while classification predicts discrete categories (needing metrics like accuracy or precision)
Classification models can never be evaluated numerically
Metric choice has nothing to do with the type of prediction being made
questions.explanation: Because regression outputs are continuous numbers and classification outputs are discrete labels, each needs metrics suited to the nature of that output.

questions.question: Why is it often useful to report more than one metric when evaluating a model?
options: A single metric always tells the complete story
Different metrics can reveal different strengths and weaknesses, and relying on just one can hide important issues
Reporting multiple metrics is only done to make results look more complex
It's required purely for legal compliance
questions.explanation: No single metric captures every aspect of performance, so looking at several together gives a more complete and honest picture of how a model is really doing.
